mcq.q: Spring frost is most damaging to the vine when it hits
choices: D Bare trunks on a grafting bench
mcq.answer: B Newly burst green shoots
mcq.why: Once buds have burst, green tissue is killed and the crop is lost.

mcq.q: A maritime climate, compared with a continental one, usually has
choices: A A shorter growing season and drier autumns
B Smaller temperature swings and rainfall spread through the year
C No risk of rain at harvest
mcq.answer: B Smaller temperature swings and rainfall spread through the year
mcq.why: Oceans buffer temperature; rain is more even — including in September.

mcq.q: High yields on a fertile site tend to produce grapes that are
choices: A More concentrated with thicker skins
B More dilute, with delayed flavour ripeness
C Always higher in tannin and colour
D Unaffected if the variety is Cabernet
mcq.answer: B More dilute, with delayed flavour ripeness
mcq.why: Too much crop delays ripening and waters down flavour and colour.

mcq.q: Vertical shoot positioning (VSP) is used mainly to
choices: A Shade all fruit in a dense hedge
B Arrange shoots in a thin curtain for light and air
C Train bush vines without wires
D Replace the need for pruning
mcq.answer: B Arrange shoots in a thin curtain for light and air
mcq.why: A tidy vertical canopy improves exposure, spray penetration and even ripening.

mcq.q: Rosé made by a short maceration on black-grape skins, then pressing, is the
choices: D Solera blending of two colours
mcq.answer: B Direct-press or short-maceration method
mcq.why: Most still rosé is a brief skin contact then a white-style ferment; saignée bleeds a tank.

mcq.q: Lees ageing in a white wine is used to add
choices: A Primary banana esters from carbonic maceration
B Texture and flavour from yeast autolysis
mcq.answer: B Texture and flavour from yeast autolysis
mcq.why: Dead yeast cells give body, creaminess and a yeasty note.

mcq.q: Acidification is most likely in
choices: B Warm-climate musts that lack natural acidity
C Sauternes after noble rot only
D Champagne base wines in a cold year
mcq.answer: B Warm-climate musts that lack natural acidity
mcq.why: Hot regions lose acid as grapes ripen; tartaric acid may be added where law allows.

mcq.q: Carbonic maceration produces a red wine that is typically
choices: A High in seed tannin and cedar oak
B Light in tannin, vividly fruity, with a banana or kirsch note
C Oxidative and nutty like Oloroso
mcq.answer: B Light in tannin, vividly fruity, with a banana or kirsch note
mcq.why: Intracellular ferment in whole berries gives colour and aroma with little tannin.

mcq.q: The 1855 classification of the Médoc ranked châteaux by
mcq.answer: B Then-current prices and reputation
mcq.why: Brokers ranked estates on price; the list has barely changed since.

mcq.q: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru Classé wines are mainly
choices: A Cabernet Sauvignon from gravel banks
B Merlot (with Cabernet Franc) from clay and limestone
mcq.answer: B Merlot (with Cabernet Franc) from clay and limestone
mcq.why: Right Bank blends, periodically reclassified, unlike Pomerol.

mcq.q: Pessac-Léognan is the inner, higher-quality zone of
choices: C Graves, for both red and dry white wines
mcq.answer: C Graves, for both red and dry white wines
mcq.why: Pessac-Léognan covers the best of northern Graves, red and white.

mcq.q: Premier Cru and Grand Cru Chablis, compared with Petit Chablis, generally come from
choices: A Portlandian soils further from the town, picked earlier
mcq.answer: B Better-exposed Kimmeridgian slopes
mcq.why: Grand and Premier Cru sit on the best Kimmeridgian aspects; Petit Chablis is often Portlandian.

mcq.q: Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet are villages of the
mcq.answer: C Côte de Beaune
mcq.why: They are the core white villages of the Côte de Beaune.

mcq.q: Pouilly-Fumé’s smoky note is often linked to
choices: B Flinty / silex soils and Sauvignon Blanc
mcq.answer: B Flinty / silex soils and Sauvignon Blanc
mcq.why: The fumé character is a local Sauvignon/soil trope, not smoke from barrels.

mcq.q: Chinon, Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil are Loire reds from
mcq.answer: C Cabernet Franc
mcq.why: Touraine Cabernet Franc: raspberry, leaf, and a cool-climate tannin.

mcq.q: Hermitage rouge is
choices: A A high-volume blended Côtes du Rhône
B A long-lived Syrah from a single steep hill
mcq.answer: B A long-lived Syrah from a single steep hill
mcq.why: The granite hill of Hermitage gives one of the Northern Rhône’s longest-lived Syrahs.

mcq.q: Gigondas is a Southern Rhône appellation whose reds are typically
choices: B Grenache-led blends similar in outline to Châteauneuf-du-Pape
mcq.answer: B Grenache-led blends similar in outline to Châteauneuf-du-Pape
mcq.why: Gigondas (and Vacqueyras) sit below CDP in fame but share GSM and warmth.

mcq.q: Vendange Tardive on an Alsace label means the grapes were
choices: A Frozen on the vine like Eiswein
B Harvested late at a legally high must weight
mcq.answer: B Harvested late at a legally high must weight
mcq.why: VT is late harvest; the wine may be dry or sweet. SGN is the botrytis selection.

mcq.q: Barbera d’Asti, compared with Barolo, is typically
choices: A Higher in tannin and paler in colour
B Deeper in colour, higher in acid, and lower in tannin
mcq.answer: B Deeper in colour, higher in acid, and lower in tannin
mcq.why: Barbera is deeply coloured, tart and relatively soft in tannin.

mcq.q: Chianti Classico must be based on
mcq.answer: B Sangiovese
mcq.why: Sangiovese is the core; small amounts of other local or international grapes are allowed.

mcq.q: Valpolicella Ripasso is made by
choices: A Fortifying the wine during ferment
B Refermenting a Valpolicella on leftover Amarone skins
C Drying grapes to full sweetness as Recioto
mcq.answer: B Refermenting a Valpolicella on leftover Amarone skins
mcq.why: Ripasso ‘re-passes’ a basic wine over Amarone pomace for extra body.

mcq.q: Gavi is a dry white from Piedmont made of
mcq.answer: A Cortese
mcq.why: Gavi DOCG is Cortese; steely, high acid, lemon.

mcq.q: Ribera del Duero reds are based on
choices: B Tempranillo, locally often called Tinto Fino
mcq.answer: B Tempranillo, locally often called Tinto Fino
mcq.why: High plateau, continental extremes, Tempranillo with a little Cabernet or Merlot.

mcq.q: Rueda’s signature white grape is
mcq.answer: B Verdejo
mcq.why: Verdejo: herbal, stone fruit, often fermented in tank for a crisp style.

mcq.q: A red Rioja Crianza must be aged for a minimum of
choices: A Six months in bottle only
B Two years in total with at least one year in oak
C Five years with two in oak
mcq.answer: B Two years in total with at least one year in oak
mcq.why: Crianza red: 2 years total, ≥1 year oak; Reserva is 3 and 1; Gran Reserva 5 and 2.

mcq.q: The Rheingau, compared with the Mosel, generally produces Riesling that is
choices: A Lighter and even lower in alcohol
B A little fuller, from warmer, more south-facing sites on the Rhine
mcq.answer: B A little fuller, from warmer, more south-facing sites on the Rhine
mcq.why: The east–west Rhine stretch gives the Rheingau more warmth than the steep Mosel.

mcq.q: Tokaji Aszú is made by
choices: A Freezing grapes on the vine and pressing while frozen
B Adding noble-rot aszú berries (or paste) to a base must or wine
C Fortifying a dry Furmint under flor
mcq.answer: B Adding noble-rot aszú berries (or paste) to a base must or wine
mcq.why: Botrytised aszú berries are macerated in must/wine, then aged.

mcq.q: Bairrada’s traditional red grape, high in tannin and acid, is
mcq.answer: B Baga
mcq.why: Baga from Bairrada: firm, age-worthy, often compared with Nebbiolo in structure.

mcq.q: Dão reds typically come from
choices: A Coastal granite sands only, always sparkling
B Granite hills, Touriga Nacional and other Portuguese varieties, moderate climate
mcq.answer: B Granite hills, Touriga Nacional and other Portuguese varieties, moderate climate
mcq.why: Dão is inland, granite, and more moderate than the Douro’s schist heat.

mcq.q: Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon is typically
choices: A Light, high-acid and always unoaked
B Full-bodied, ripe, and often matured in a high proportion of new oak
mcq.answer: B Full-bodied, ripe, and often matured in a high proportion of new oak
mcq.why: Warm, sunny Napa gives ripe Cabernet; new French oak is common at the quality end.

mcq.q: Casablanca Valley is valued in Chile for
choices: A The hottest Cabernet sites in Maipo
B Cool coastal influence suited to Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay
C Altitude above 2,000 m like Uco
mcq.answer: B Cool coastal influence suited to Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay
mcq.why: Pacific and Humboldt influence keep Casablanca (and San Antonio) cool.

mcq.q: Barossa Valley Shiraz is typically
choices: A Pale, minty and low in alcohol like Coonawarra Cabernet
B Full, ripe, often from old bush vines in a warm climate
mcq.answer: B Full, ripe, often from old bush vines in a warm climate
mcq.why: Warm Barossa and old dry-grown vines give plush, high-alcohol Shiraz.

mcq.q: Central Otago is known for
choices: A Maritime Sauvignon Blanc like Marlborough
B Continental Pinot Noir in New Zealand’s south
mcq.answer: B Continental Pinot Noir in New Zealand’s south
mcq.why: Inland, high, continental: New Zealand’s ripest, most structured Pinot.

mcq.q: French IGP (for example Pays d’Oc) compared with AOC generally allows
choices: A No variety names on the label
B A wider area and more freedom of variety and method
C Stricter yield and ageing rules
mcq.answer: B A wider area and more freedom of variety and method
mcq.why: IGP is the PGI tier: larger zones, more varieties, variety-led labels.

mcq.q: Rioja and Priorat share Spain’s top legal tier, which is
mcq.answer: B DOCa / DOQ
mcq.why: Only Rioja and Priorat are DOCa/DOQ.

mcq.q: On an EU still-wine label, if a vintage is stated, the usual minimum from that year is
mcq.why: EU rule is 85% for vintage (and for a stated variety), unless a stricter local law applies.

mcq.q: Vintage Champagne must spend a minimum of
mcq.answer: C 36 months on lees
mcq.why: Vintage: 36 months on lees; NV: 15.

mcq.q: The Vallée de la Marne is particularly planted with
choices: A Chardonnay on pure chalk only
B Pinot Meunier, which buds later and ripens more reliably in frost-prone sites
C Only Arbane and Petit Meslier
mcq.answer: B Pinot Meunier, which buds later and ripens more reliably in frost-prone sites
mcq.why: Meunier’s later budburst and earlier ripeness suit the frost-prone valley.

mcq.q: Cava’s second fermentation takes place
choices: B In bottle, by the traditional method
mcq.answer: B In bottle, by the traditional method
mcq.why: Cava is traditional method; lees time is legally defined (longer for Reserva/Gran Reserva).

mcq.q: Asti (the fully sparkling DOCG) is typically
choices: A Bone-dry, high alcohol, traditional method
B Low alcohol, sweet, tank method from Moscato Bianco
C A rosé from Pinot Noir only
mcq.answer: B Low alcohol, sweet, tank method from Moscato Bianco
mcq.why: One ferment in tank is stopped to keep sugar and about 7–9.5% abv.

mcq.q: Crémant de Loire is made by
choices: A The tank method from Glera
B The traditional method, often from Chenin Blanc and/or Cabernet Franc
C The ancestral method only in Limoux
mcq.answer: B The traditional method, often from Chenin Blanc and/or Cabernet Franc
mcq.why: French Crémants are traditional method; Loire uses local grapes, not Glera.

mcq.q: Manzanilla may be aged only in
choices: B El Puerto de Santa María
mcq.answer: C Sanlúcar de Barrameda
mcq.why: The cooler, humid Sanlúcar air keeps flor thicker; the name is legally tied to the town.

mcq.q: A 20-year-old Tawny Port is aged
choices: A In bottle from the second year like Vintage
B Oxidatively in wood for a long period, then bottled ready to drink
D On skins in a closed tank for 20 years
mcq.answer: B Oxidatively in wood for a long period, then bottled ready to drink
mcq.why: Tawny categories (10/20/30/40) are wood-aged, nutty, and do not need decanting for sediment.

mcq.q: Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) Port, compared with Vintage Port, is usually
choices: A Aged longer in wood (about 4–6 years) and released ready to drink
B Aged only in bottle from the first spring
D Never from a single year
mcq.answer: A Aged longer in wood (about 4–6 years) and released ready to drink
mcq.why: LBV is a single year kept in wood longer so it is approachable on release.

mcq.q: Oloroso Sherry is aged
choices: A Under a complete flor covering
B Oxidatively, without flor, after fortification to a higher strength
C In bottle on its lees
mcq.answer: B Oxidatively, without flor, after fortification to a higher strength
mcq.why: Fortify to about 17% so flor cannot grow; oxygen builds walnut and toffee notes.

mcq.q: Rutherglen Muscat is
choices: A A dry table wine from Victoria’s cool south
B A fortified, oxidatively aged sweet Muscat from north-east Victoria
C A tank sparkling from Glera
mcq.answer: B A fortified, oxidatively aged sweet Muscat from north-east Victoria
mcq.why: Rutherglen’s heat and solera-like ageing give raisin, tea and toffee Muscats.

mcq.q: Volatile acidity as a fault smells of
choices: C Struck match that lifts with air
mcq.answer: B Vinegar and/or nail-varnish remover
mcq.why: Acetic acid and ethyl acetate define VA when they dominate.

mcq.q: Full-bodied oaked white wines (for example Meursault) are best served
choices: C At 18–20 °C like a tannic red
mcq.answer: B Lightly chilled, about 10–13 °C
mcq.why: Too cold hides oak and texture; too warm makes alcohol clumsy.

mcq.q: A very sweet dessert needs a wine that is
choices: B At least as sweet as the dish, or the wine will taste thin
C High in tannin and bone dry
mcq.answer: B At least as sweet as the dish, or the wine will taste thin
mcq.why: If the food is sweeter than the wine, the wine tastes sour and bitter.

mcq.q: The SAT quality scale, from lowest to highest acceptable wine, ends at
choices: A Good, then Very Good, then Outstanding
B Acceptable, then Premium, then Icon
mcq.answer: A Good, then Very Good, then Outstanding
mcq.why: Faulty / Poor / Acceptable / Good / Very Good / Outstanding — judged on BLIC, not liking.

parts.prompt: Contrast climate, topography and soils of the Northern Rhône with those of the Southern Rhône.
points: North: moderate continental, steep granite/schist slopes, the river and mistral; vineyards in a narrow corridor.
South: warmer Mediterranean, flatter or garrigue hills, galets/sand/clay, more drought and heat.
North is almost all hillside Syrah (and a little white); south is a broad plain of blends.
Mistral dries and cools both, but the south is still distinctly warmer.
Named AOCs as illustration: Côte-Rôtie/Hermitage vs Châteauneuf/Gigondas.
Award for harvest-rain vs drought, or for the role of the river.

parts.prompt: State the principal grape varieties of each zone and the style of one named red appellation from each.
points: North red: Syrah. Whites: Viognier (Condrieu, Château-Grillet); Marsanne and Roussanne (Hermitage, Crozes, Saint-Péray).
Côte-Rôtie may include a little co-fermented Viognier.
South red: Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and others (GSM); whites from Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne, etc.
Example north: Hermitage — full, tannic, black fruit, pepper, long-lived.
Example south: Châteauneuf-du-Pape — ripe, often higher alcohol, spice, garrigue.
Tavel as rosé-only can score as extra.

parts.prompt: Describe typical red winemaking in Côte-Rôtie or Hermitage versus a high-volume Côtes du Rhône.
points: Quality north: hand harvest, sort, destem (some whole bunch in Côte-Rôtie), ferment on skins, punch down/pump over.
Maceration for colour and ripe tannin; MLF; 12–24 months in oak (a mix of new and old, 228 L or larger).
Côtes du Rhône volume: machine harvest possible, short maceration, stainless or large old wood, little new oak, earlier release.
Southern quality wines may use concrete, large foudres, and a Grenache-friendly warmer ferment.
Whole-bunch and Viognier co-ferment as northern options.
State the style result: structured, age-worthy vs fruity, early-drinking.

parts.prompt: Outline the climate of inland Tuscany and the vineyard factors that affect Sangiovese quality.
points: Warm Mediterranean with continental touches inland; altitude (Chianti Classico hills, Montalcino) cools nights and keeps acid.
Galestro and alberese soils in Chianti; Montalcino often warmer and drier.
Sangiovese is late ripening, thin-skinned, high acid, needs a long season and careful site choice.
Yield control is vital; too much crop gives pale, tart wine.
Aspect and height separate Chianti Classico from broader Chianti.
Frost less of an issue than in the north; drought and heat spikes matter in warm years.

parts.prompt: Compare Chianti Classico with Brunello di Montalcino in law, grapes and typical style.
points: Chianti Classico: Sangiovese-based (high minimum %), other local/international grapes allowed; Riserva and Gran Selezione tiers.
Brunello: 100% Sangiovese (Brunello), longer minimum ageing, usually more expensive.
Chianti Classico: red cherry, high acid, firm but not extreme tannin, often some oak.
Brunello: fuller, more structured, longer-lived, released later.
Geography: Classico is the historic limestone hills between Florence and Siena; Montalcino is further south.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano as a third Sangiovese DOCG can score.

parts.prompt: Describe winemaking choices that turn Sangiovese into a wine suitable for ageing, and name one risk if extraction is too harsh.
points: Ripe, sorted fruit; destem; ferment on skins with enough but not brutal extraction.
Temperature control; punch down/pump over; length of maceration matched to seed ripeness.
MLF; oak — large Slavonian botti and/or French barriques; time in wood and bottle per DOCG rules.
Over-extraction or unripe seeds give bitter, drying tannin that fruit and acid cannot balance.
New barriques can mask cherry fruit if overused.
Mention of government ageing minima for Brunello/Riserva can score.

parts.prompt: Compare the production method, grapes and typical style of Prosecco with those of Cava.
points: Prosecco: Glera; tank / Martinotti–Charmat second ferment; primary pear, apple, floral; usually extra dry or brut; drink young.
Conegliano-Valdobbiadene DOCG and Asolo vs wider Prosecco DOC; Rive and Cartizze as quality mentions.
Cava: Macabeo, Xarel-lo, Parellada (plus Chardonnay/Pinot); traditional method; autolytic notes if aged longer.
Most Cava from Catalonia; Reserva/Gran Reserva longer on lees.
Style: Prosecco is fruit-first and softer in acidity; Cava is usually drier in feel, more citrus and toast when aged.
Award for mentioning Col Fondo / ancestral as a minority Prosecco style.

parts.prompt: Why is the tank method well suited to a variety such as Glera?
points: Glera’s appeal is primary fruit and flower, not autolysis.
Tank is faster and cheaper; wine can be released young.
Pressure and temperature are easy to control; residual sugar can be adjusted.
Bottle-method cost and lees character would hide Glera’s point.
Large volumes for a global brand need an industrial but clean process.

parts.prompt: Give service advice for a Brut Cava Reserva and one food match, with a reason.
points: Serve well chilled (about 6–10 °C) in a flute or white-wine glass.
Open carefully; no need to decant.
Drink on release; Gran Reserva can take a little bottle age.
Food: fried fish, salty snacks, or light tapas — bubbles and acid cut fat and salt.
Avoid very sweet desserts unless the Cava is demi-sec.
Award for contrasting Extra Dry Prosecco with lightly sweet fruit dishes.

parts.prompt: Describe the Douro’s vineyard conditions and how they influence grapes used for Port.
points: Hot, dry, continental summers; schist terraces (socalcos, patamares) above the Douro.
Low rainfall in the growing season; irrigation limited; low yields.
Three sub-zones: Baixo Corgo (coolest, wettest), Cima Corgo (heart), Douro Superior (hottest, driest).
Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão and others.
Thick skins and high sugar from heat suit a sweet fortified red.
Field blends and old vines are still common.

parts.prompt: Outline the making of Vintage Port and of a 10-year-old Tawny, and contrast their ageing.
points: Foot-treading or modern plungers in lagares for colour and tannin in a short ferment.
Fortify to about 19–22% with grape spirit while sugar remains; run off skins.
Vintage: best lots, declared in outstanding years; about 2 years in wood; bottled unfiltered; ages in bottle for decades; heavy sediment.
10-year Tawny: wood-aged oxidatively, blended to an average age; bottled ready; nutty, dried fruit, paler.
Vintage needs decanting; tawny does not (for sediment).
LBV and Colheita as linking styles can score.

parts.prompt: Recommend storage and a food pairing for each style.
points: Vintage: store on its side, cool and dark, for years; stand up then decant before service; serve slightly cool (about 16 °C).
Tawny: store upright once bottled for service; serve lightly chilled; lasts weeks after opening if cool.
Vintage with blue cheese or dark chocolate; tawny with nut tart or crème caramel.
Sweetness of the wine must meet the dish.
Do not cellar an open tawny like a sealed vintage bottle.
